speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: One in two Singapore residents is expected to develop severe disability at some point in their lifetime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: CareShield Life, our national long-term care insurance scheme, was launched in 2020 to provide basic financial protection against long-term care costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: It is an integral part of our long-term care financing framework and sits alongside other layers of support that work together to help those with long-term care needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: These include: Government subsidies for nursing homes, as well as home-based and community-based care; grants such as the Home Caregiving Grant and Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund; MediSave withdrawals for long-term care; and safety nets such as ElderFund and MediFund.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: As an insurance scheme, CareShield Life works on the basis of risk-pooling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This means that each birth cohort pays premiums that go towards meeting the claims of those from that cohort who might develop severe disability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This approach allows us to come together to support one another's future needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: It is also a more sustainable approach, as every cohort pays premiums that go towards supporting the long-term care needs of that cohort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: CareShield Life covers all Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents born in 1980 and later, from when they turn 30.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This is regardless of pre-existing disabilities or health conditions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: For those born in 1979 and earlier, we encourage them to enrol in CareShield Life, but kept participation optional when CareShield Life was first launched in 2020, as their circumstances and needs could vary widely and they may have already made their own plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This is the group we term as the Optional Cohort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Currently, new Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents born in 1979 and earlier are also covered under CareShield Life if they are not severely disabled when they become a Citizen or Permanent Resident.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Under CareShield Life, policyholders pay premiums from their age of entry until age 67, or for up to 10 years, whichever is longer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: If policyholders are assessed to be of severe disability, or in other words, unable to perform at least three out of six Activities of Daily Living (ADLs), they will receive monthly cash payouts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: These ADLs include washing, dressing, feeding, toileting, walking or moving around and transferring between bed and chair.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Upon successful claims, if the individual had still been paying premiums, he or she will no longer need to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Policyholders receive cash payouts for as long as they remain in severe disability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: The Council released its recommendations in August 2025, after extensive public engagement and careful deliberation, with its recommendations accepted in full by the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: The increased payouts will better cushion against rising long-term care costs driven by inflation of manpower and technology costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: For younger policyholders, the benefits are even more significant over time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Take, for example, a 30-year-old who joins CareShield Life in 2026.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Should he or she make a claim at age 70, the payout will be $2,940 per month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This is more than double the payout of $1,406 per month under the current lower growth rate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: The Council also recommended adjusting premiums to sustain the higher payouts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Without this support, premiums in 2026 would have increased by approximately $126 on average, with a 4% per annum increase thereafter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: To keep premiums affordable and fair, the Council has also recommended adjusting CareShield Life's underwriting criteria, as planned earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: I will explain this in greater detail later.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: These CareShield Life enhancements complement the long-term care subsidy and grant enhancements announced at Budget 2025, where we will be raising subsidies for long-term care services, to up to 80% for nursing homes and 95% for home and community care services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: We are also expanding the eligibility criteria to cover seven in 10 households, so that more can benefit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: We will increase Home Caregiving Grant cash payouts from a maximum of $400 to a higher maximum value of $600 and will expand the coverage of the Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: These enhancements will be progressively implemented from January 2026.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: To illustrate the impact, consider a CareShield Life policyholder with a per capita household income of $1,500.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Together, the enhanced subsidies and grants will help to offset more than two-thirds of their community-based long-term care costs, with the enhanced CareShield Life payouts covering another quarter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: After the financing support, the patient's individual out-of-pocket expenses will come down to $110 per month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: The enhancements to CareShield Life, as well as Government subsidy and grant schemes will collectively provide Singaporeans with greater assurance that long-term care will remain affordable for years to come.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: To implement the Council's recommendations I have just outlined, amendments to the Act are necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This Bill makes targeted amendments to two key areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: First, we will reinstate the planned underwriting criterion for Optional Cohorts and new Singapore Citizens or Permanent Residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This reinstatement was planned for right from when the scheme was first launched.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This move will help moderate premiums for the older CareShield Life policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Second, we will strengthen our premium recovery processes to ensure the scheme's sustainability and fairness to all policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: As I mentioned, CareShield Life is kept optional for those born in 1979 or earlier, the Optional Cohorts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This was a considered decision that recognised that many Singaporeans in these cohorts may have already made alternative arrangements for their long-term care needs before CareShield Life was introduced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: They might also be enrolled in ElderShield, which was the earlier long-term care insurance scheme, later replaced by CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: For the Optional Cohorts, they would also have had to pay higher annual premiums, as they would be enrolling at a later age and have fewer years to pay the premiums needed to support their lifetime benefits under the scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Nonetheless, the Government welcomed them to join if they wished to enrol, for greater assurance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: We had outreach campaigns and offered participation incentives to encourage them to join.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: We also relaxed the underwriting criteria as a time-limited measure, so even those who already had mild to moderate disability, could enrol.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: I want to emphasise that once insurance take-up is optional, underwriting is important.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This is to guard against adverse selection where those who are more likely to claim will be more likely to enrol, driving up claims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Therefore, when the scheme was first conceptualised, it was designed such that only Optional Cohort individuals without any pre-existing disability could enrol in the scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: However, the Ministry of Health (MOH) decided to grant a time-limited concession to keep the scheme inclusive at its launch.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Under this concession, any Optional Cohort individual without severe disability, including those with milder forms of disability, could enrol in and benefit from the scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Participation incentives of up to $4,000 were also offered to offset premiums and to encourage enrolment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: With this approach, we have seen many from the Optional Cohort opting to join CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: When CareShield Life was first launched in 2020, we announced that the concession period would be for two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: However, we allowed it to run for twice as long, or about four years, as we recognised that enrolment in CareShield Life might not have been top of mind for Singaporeans during the COVID-19 years that the initial concession was timed for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Since then, sign-ups are now almost 90% lower than when the scheme was first launched for the Optional Cohorts in 2021 and have levelled off.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This adjustment will benefit all Optional Cohort policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Remember I said earlier that risk-pooling is cohort-based.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: So, the risk is taken on and the cost is borne by those in their cohorts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: With the earlier concession, premiums had to be set higher to account for the possibility that Optional Cohort individuals with mild to moderate disabilities might be more likely to join CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Now that the underwriting criterion will be reinstated, this risk is reduced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This allows premiums to be moderated, keeping the scheme fair and sustainable for all policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: The Bill implements these changes through several key provisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Clauses 2(a) and 8 introduce a new definition of "not disabled" in the Act, with the detailed meaning set out in a new Fourth Schedule.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: The Schedule defines "not disabled" as being able to perform all six ADLs without assistance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This provides the foundation for our reinstated underwriting criterion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Clause 6 provides the Minister with powers to amend this Fourth Schedule by order published in the Gazette.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Any such order must be presented to Parliament after publication for proper oversight.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Clause 3 amends the underwriting criterion or eligibility criteria for CareShield Life under section 6 of the CareShield Life and Long-Term Care Act 2019 which applies to New Singapore Citizens or Permanent Residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This means that they have no pre-existing disability and are able to perform all six ADLs independently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: We will be amending the relevant regulations so that this underwriting criterion of being "not disabled" will, likewise, apply to the Optional Cohorts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: In implementing these changes, I want to assure Members that we remain committed to fairness, inclusivity and sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: The Optional Cohorts have had sufficient time, four years, to join CareShield Life under the more inclusive underwriting criterion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: The adjustment of underwriting criterion applies only to new Optional Cohort enrolment from 1 January 2026.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Existing policyholders will see no change to their coverage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Importantly, those with pre-existing disability can continue to benefit from other Government financing schemes, such as long-term care subsidies and grants, including the Home Caregiving Grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Like any other insurance scheme, CareShield Life relies on collective responsibility through risk-pooling within each cohort to provide policyholders with peace of mind in the event of severe disability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: As part of this collective responsibility, all policyholders must play their part by meeting their premium obligations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This ensures that CareShield Life can continue to support potential claimants in a timely and sustainable manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: So, this will be something we want to give assurance to all our Citizens and our residents here in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: However, there are also some individuals who can afford to, but wilfully decide not to pay their premiums despite repeated reminders and eventually become defaulters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Owed premiums that cannot be recovered will affect CareShield Life Fund's financial sustainability and ultimately affect CareShield Life's ability to meet its claims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Premium recovery and enforcement measures are, therefore, needed to ensure fairness for all policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: To support these recovery efforts, clause 5 of the Bill introduces the new section 61A to scope the modes through which demand notes may be effectively served.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Demand notes are formal notices served to defaulters stating their outstanding premiums and any interest imposed that is payable by the defaulter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: These demand notes are a key enabler to our premium recovery process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Demand notes will be served before recovery measures can commence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Such recovery measures may include imposing interests or penalties, or appointing agents to recover outstanding premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: The current provisions enable demand notes to be served through various channels, including registered mail.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: However, we face operational challenges when policyholders fail to update their addresses or reside overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This often makes it difficult to reach them through traditional postal methods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Such an effort is in line with the overall move across the Government to complement, not replace, physical touchpoints with digital channels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: These amendments will also align the approach with similar provisions already in place for MediShield Life and will improve operational efficiency and streamline premium recovery actions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Those with genuine difficulties affording their premiums will continue to be supported by premium support measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Together with the substantial subsidy and grant enhancements announced at Budget 2025, these amendments and the changes to CareShield Life will continue to provide Singaporeans with the assurance they need as they age.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The caregiving needs will increase given smaller families shouldering the burden of caregiving and long-term care costs rising faster than general inflation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In Jalan Kayu and beyond, I have met families struggling to balance between caregiving, work and the costs of care.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Expenses for helpers and nursing homes can run into thousands per month.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Even with subsidies, many middle-income households feel the strain.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Caregivers often worry about how long they can keep going – physically, emotionally and financially.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: They want their loved ones to be given the best care in the best way possible.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: That is why I agree this Bill matters.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must ensure that CareShield Life gives real assurance to families when severe disabilities strike, that both the stricken person and their caregiver will have the support they need.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Today, I would like to touch on three areas: payout adequacy, premium affordability and, in conjunction with CareShield Life, refresh our "Caregiver Compact" so that caregivers themselves are supported even as they care for their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We know that long-term care costs are rising faster than general inflation.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But the key question remains: will payouts keep pace with actual costs of long-term care in the years ahead?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: To help Singaporeans plan ahead with confidence, I suggest pegging payouts to cover at least a certain proportion of long-term care costs.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: In other words, make the payout percentages to the estimated long-term care costs clearer.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This would give families a clearer, better picture of what CareShield Life will cover and, importantly as well, what it will not cover so that they can plan early for the rest of care needs through other sources or supplementary plans.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I also seek clarity on the stopping of payout growth after age 67 or once claims are made.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Without continued payout growth, CareShield Life can fall short just when families need it most, as inflation steadily chips away at the real value of the payouts.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I hope the Minister can share how the Government will ensure that payouts will remain meaningful and adequate during the extended years when the payout is needed.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Because at its very heart, like what the Minister has mentioned, this is not just about the policy design, but assuring and giving ordinary Singaporeans peace of mind knowing that the premiums they have paid, faithfully, over the years will translate into real assurance when CareShield Life payouts are needed most.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: My second point is on the affordability of premiums.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I am heartened by the Senior Minister of State's repeated assurance that no one will lose coverage because they cannot afford their premiums.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This assurance matters deeply and I am glad I heard the Minister say two, if not three times.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: But even so, for many middle-income families, including those in Jalan Kayu who may not qualify for means-tested support, the worry is still real and remains.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: To give families greater assurance, I suggest that premiums be capped at a fixed percentage of the median per capita household income.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This ensures premiums remain fair and sustainable, in line with wage growth over longer periods of time.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: It would also help if the Government could indicate what is the expected upper limit of premiums beyond 2030, so that Singaporeans can plan their finances with greater certainty.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Pegging payouts and managing premiums in tandem would give Singaporeans a stronger sense of predictability and stability, knowing both what they can expect in payout support on the one hand and what premiums contribution is needed on the other hand.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This clarity will go a long way in helping families plan responsibly without the anxiety of being overwhelmed when the care needs arise.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must ensure that caregivers themselves are not left behind.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: There are many areas of support we can and must strengthen.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Today, I want to focus on one – helping caregivers build up their own retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Many of our caregivers, especially and often women, spend years caring for loved ones, especially those who become severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Many make the difficult decision to leave the workforce.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: As a result, they may have smaller CPF balances and savings.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Later in life, they may well struggle to afford the long-term care they themselves need.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: We must not let those who provided care in their younger years go without care in their own old age.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I urge the Government to consider providing CPF top-ups to primary caregivers who lack retirement savings due to caregiving.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: This would go some way in giving them assurance that even as they care for others, they, too, will be cared for in turn.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: I hope the Government can refresh the action plan to better recognise caregivers' sacrifices, strengthen the ecosystem around them and help them care for both their loved ones and, in time, for themselves.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: (In Mandarin):   The elderly around us have quietly dedicated themselves to bringing us up.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Now that we have grown up, we should remember our roots and safeguard their twilight years.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: The CareShield Life scheme is an important pillar of our nation's long-term care system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Care recipients are our parents, our partners, our neighbours and perhaps, even ourselves.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Every Singaporean hopes that when frailty comes, they can look to a system of support which includes not only from family and loved ones but from the society that we live in, through a national system that spreads the risk equitably, offers dignity and lightens the load on those who give care.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As a developed, wealthy country, the principle of shared responsibility through CareShield Life should rightly form one of the key pillars of our social safety net, providing financial support for Singaporeans faced with severe disability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is why the Workers' Party (WP) has supported it conceptually since its inception in 2020.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As the scheme matures and as our society continues to age, we must ensure that it continues to embody the spirit of fairness and solidarity that should be a bedrock of a truly caring society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Where we can do more, we must do more.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: CareShield Life marked a shift from its predecessor, ElderShield, by extending coverage to provide for lifetime monthly payouts from when an insured becomes severely disabled and becoming compulsory for younger cohorts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Since CareShield Life was first debated in Parliament in 2018, we have seen significant increases in the cost of living off the back of global events like the pandemic, wars and geopolitical tensions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The increase from 2% to 4% of the annual growth rate of CareShield Life payouts is, thus, welcome as an acknowledgement that long-term care costs have outpaced inflation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given that long-term care costs have been outpacing general inflation since, the increase in payouts will be welcome by families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, could the Minister explain ongoing and future monitoring mechanisms and calculations for Singaporeans, as policyholders, to better understand what would be taken into consideration for the Government to once again assess whether the current payouts will be adequate?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, we can anticipate that any future increases in payout rates would also have consequent increases in premiums and, thus, a direct impact on Singaporeans as we continue to age.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, I would like to repeat the call made by the Leader of the Opposition Pritam Singh in his speech when CareShield Life was introduced and debated in this House in 2018, where he asked the Government to reveal actuarial principles and to publish investment returns and premium adjustment factors regularly.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On premiums, I note that while premiums will go up to support the changes to the scheme, the Government has put in place various support measures.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, I wish to, today, again bring up the issue of gender-differentiated premiums because how we price care says something about how we value those who provide it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is not a new point and WP Members of Parliament (MPs) shared their concerns about this when CareShield Life was introduced in this House in 2018.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Women pay higher premiums, and this is still the case, with the reasoning that women live longer and claim more.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given that CareShield Life has been running for five years now and the Ministry would, presumably, now have some data about claimants under the plan, could the Minister share whether the assumptions that women would claim more and for longer have been borne out?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even if the actuarial reasoning and data makes sense, actuarial fairness is not always the same as social fairness.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Applying a strict actuarial lens when deciding to charge women more for enrolment in this compulsory plan does not take into account the following factors.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, women in Singapore have lower lifetime earnings and smaller CPF balances on average.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is widely accepted that career decisions have a significant impact on the gender pay difference and that societal, cultural or even biological factors mean that women in Singapore continue to shoulder more caregiving work compared with men.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is often the default position that women are the ones who reduce their working hours, turn down promotions or increased responsibilities at work, or even leave the workforce altogether in order to care for a parent, spouse, child; sacrificing income, retirement adequacy and sometimes, even at the expense of their own health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Add to this, that globally, women live longer but spend more years in ill health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Closing this gender health gap could add over US$3 billion annually to Singapore's gross domestic product (GDP) by 2040.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, when we ask this very same group, women, to pay more for CareShield Life, we risk deepening structural inequities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The caregiver who has spent years enabling others to work is in effect asked to bear a greater cost for the very care safety net her unpaid labour helps sustain.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This can also be compounded by findings in jurisdictions, like New South Wales in Australia, which noticed that while both women and men experienced disability at similar rates, women only made up 37% of claimants of its national disability insurance scheme.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One of the more sobering findings was that because women shoulder more of the care work in the family, they end up with less time to manage their own disabilities and take on the administrative work associated with disability claims.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could the Senior Minister of State clarify whether a similar picture exists in Singapore and if so, what is being done to address this additional challenge?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just as importantly, by making women pay more, are we sending a signal that society does not provide for both men and women at the same rate?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When a woman reduces work hours to care for an ageing parent or a disabled relative, she loses income, retirement savings and then pays higher premiums for this privilege of having provided that unpaid care.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In view of the above, I hope that we could consider the following: first, greater transparency; second, mandatory periodic review triggers of premium structures; third, explore how best we can close the gender gap.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On transparency, the Ministry should publish actuarial data regularly, including average claim duration, payout levels and fund solvency, as it currently does, to a certain extent, for MediShield Life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Publishing such data of what is, after all, a national insurance scheme will allow the public to be better understand the financial reasons as to why policy shifts occur when they do and to equip us, in this House, with a full picture as we strive to understand the trade-offs to be made within the policy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, given that we are announcing the doubling of payout increases five years after the scheme started, I believe that it would help the public to understand at what point we would need to, again, review the adequacy of payouts, given changing costs of care.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If this narrowing of life expectancy between men and women continues and if we were to succeed in our aims to close the gender health gap, it would be remiss not to ask whether there is still a place for gender-based pricing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We, therefore, hope that the Government can commit to reviewing this policy when a specific threshold is crossed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This could take the form of a review of gender-based premiums that gets triggered when the differences in payouts narrow to a specific threshold on average over a few years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The exact threshold should be determined by actuarists with access to full data and the threshold should be published.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And when that threshold is crossed, a mandatory review of the existing policy should take place.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, MediShield Life already does so, and we should explore how CareShield Life can be structured to phase towards this approach once we have adequate claims experience available.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If we accept that CareShield Life is a national insurance rather than a commercial insurance product, given the constraints that women face, there is value in building equity into the design of the scheme rather than attempt to patch up any inequalities using subsidies or ad hoc support of cash offsets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A baseline protection against disability should be universally accessible to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And inherently, it does not sit right to penalise a group, that is, women, by making us pay more for what are often factors beyond our control.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, globally, it has been found that women have a higher prevalence of disabling conditions, such as arthritis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And to achieve our aims towards a Healthier SG, I hope, too, that we continue to work on various preventative and early intervention initiatives to address the various health challenges that women face, to do what we can to minimise women's time in ill health and address these concerns about a double or even triple whammy facing women as we age.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These suggestions are not about favouring one group over another; they are about ensuring that the principle of shared risk applies equally to everyone and to address any systemic issues at the root that may be causing the inequity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our goal should not be to rebalance inequity with subsidies but to explore how we can remove inequity from the structure itself.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given this is a finite group who already currently live with severe disabilities, I would like to seek clarification on what support would be available to these individuals who may in the future be faced with an unexpected exigency, for example, in the form of suddenly losing coverage under their own plans, which were meant to cover their long-term care needs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this case, would the Ministry be willing to consider any appeals on an exceptional basis to be included in the scheme after the reinstatement?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For many families, day-to-day realities and challenges of caring for loved ones means a constant juggling of the invisible mental load and unpaid work involved in caregiving, arranging for services, balancing work while simultaneously facing exhaustion and burnout.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And for caregivers who take on much unpaid and unseen work, it bears reiterating what my colleague Aljunied group representation constituency (GRC) MP Gerald Giam said during this year’s Committee of Supply debate, that care recipients and carers have different needs and that our support system needs to reflect this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These details alone should cause alarm, and we must urgently build stronger, more holistic support, with solutions that better capture and respond to the time, skill and emotional resilience needed in their unpaid care work.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This can take the form of accessible interventions targeted at realities rather than add to their workload, whether it is in form of mental health support or rallying better social connections within our communities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Underscoring this, during the launch of our Caregivers’ Wishes initiatives last week, we heard many stories from Singaporean carers and recipients, with a common thread of caregivers needing not only more financial support, but more time, more skills and more understanding.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Giving this support is not charity, it is an investment into our society’s care resilience.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A truly caring nation should not measure support in actuarial tables only, but in how we treat and support those who give and those who need care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: You cannot walk, you cannot dress yourself or feed yourself.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Your body fails you, slowly, while your savings drain away.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This could happen to any of us or to someone we love.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That is why long-term care is not a “someday” issue.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When CareShield Life was lauched, it was a bold, necessary move, one that showed the foresight of this Government in planning for our ageing society.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Council’s recommendations and the Bill before us today takes the next step: enhancing payouts, adjusting premiums and tightening administration to keep pace with rising care needs and healthcare costs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we reﬁne the mechanics, we must ask deeper questions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I will speak today on ﬁve areas we must strengthen – system coherence, affordability and payout adequacy, inter-generational fairness, coverage, and long-term care delivery on the ground.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Long-term care sits alongside Healthier SG, Age Well SG, S+3M framework, Home Caregiving Grant and other support schemes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is an opportunity and a need to strengthen the linkages between these schemes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, long-term care is a bit of a jigsaw puzzle with pieces from different boxes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And families, especially middle-income households, sometimes ﬁnd community-based care harder to access or less supported.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We encourage Singaporeans to get screened, exercise and join Healthier SG.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But those who do the right thing do not seem to see any tangible beneﬁts here – no premium discounts, rebates, not even Healthy365 points.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What we need is a continuum of care that connects prevention, early intervention and long-term care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This means standardising assessment, aligning payouts, subsidies and incentives, and making it easier for families to choose the right care, with structured pathways with less bureaucracy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, offering premium rebates for active participation in Healthier SG programmes or automatically bundling CareShield Life payouts with Age Well SG community services.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The CareShield Life Council, Healthier SG Office and Age Well SG agencies can be tasked to jointly look at how prevention and community care trends impact ﬁnancing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This kind of system coherence aligns incentives across a person’s life course, so that we bend the cost curve, not just chase it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For lower- to middle-income families supporting multiple dependants and those with lower MediSave balances, such as retirees and the self-employed, this can be a strain.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A middle-income household with a per capita income of just over $3,600 but below $4,800 today gets no CareShield Life premium subsidy, even though they will later qualify for long-term care subsidies if disability strikes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This may make sense within individual schemes, but to families on the ground, it feels inconsistent and the “sandwiched middle” shoulders a heavier burden upfront.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will the Ministry consider increasing the subsidy income threshold so that greater alignment between ﬁnancing and service subsidies exist across premium support, care subsidies and Healthier SG and Age Well SG programmes?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A coherent, transparent framework will help families plan better and strengthen trust in the system.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For those with very low MediSave balances, the Additional Premium Support scheme is critical.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State share how much Additional Premium Support has been disbursed so far and what is budgeted for the next ﬁve years?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will the Minister consider expanding Additional Premium Support to ensure no one loses CareShield coverage due to affordability?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And I am heartened to hear the Senior Minister of State speak and reiterate that many times in his speech.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: On payouts, 4% annual payout increases may not keep pace with actual long-term care cost inﬂation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And since the payout is also ﬁxed at the point of claim or at age 67, their value may erode over time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will the Ministry consider regular affordability reviews to monitor premiums, subsidies, payouts and inﬂation, and recalibrate quickly as needed?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we debate premiums and payouts, we must also look at inter-generational fairness.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Younger Singaporeans are paying into CareShield Life, putting trust in a promise: that the system will protect them when they need it most.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And let us not forget that some will never make a claim.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Still, they contribute to make the system work for all.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet disability rates and care costs could rise faster than current actuarial assumptions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will the Majulah Generation and younger Singaporeans be looking at substantial premium increases over their lifetimes?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will coverage still be sufficient when their time comes?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To preserve trust, can the Ministry commit to monitoring actuarial assumptions closely and adjusting premiums gradually and with transparency, integrating prevention with long-term care ﬁnancing models?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Seniors who were too old, had pre-existing disabilities, even mild ones, or were not yet Singapore Citizens or Permanent Residents at the time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: People like my Woodlands resident, Mdm T, who told me quietly, “I’m not afraid of dying, I’m afraid of being a burden to my children.” She is not alone.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Seniors who are excluded from MediShield Life, may have to rely on family or minimal social assistance.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet these are the very people most likely to need long-term care soon.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Schemes, like the Interim Disability Assistance Programme for Elderly (IDAPE), help but only partially.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This underwriting gap is a coverage gap and a fairness gap.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Or creating targeted risk pools or options for partial entry for excluded seniors, even if it means smaller payouts rather than this all-or-nothing coverage?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: No senior should be left unprotected simply because they were born too early or became disabled too soon.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Even the best ﬁnancing design means little if services on the ground are stretched and wait times are long, whether it is for a nursing home bed, home personal care or caregiver services, including respite care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In Woodlands, new facilities like Ren Ci at Woodlands Health Campus have added beds and day places.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But waiting times for some services still run weeks and longer for specialised care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When my Woodlands resident had to look for a nursing home for his brother, he had to put him in a nursing home in Jurong for the fastest enrolment, which means higher travel time and cost for the family.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Families should not have to choose between speed and proximity when it comes to long-term care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Let us build a long-term care system that does not just protects today’s seniors, but keeps faith with today’s young and stands strong for generations yet to come.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because how we care for the most vulnerable around us is a true test of the “we first” society that we are building together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I support the Bill but will share some remarks on the first element, dealing with the scope of coverage of CareShield Life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will begin with elements close to the specificities of this present Bill, before moving on to more general issues of coverage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This would, effectively, compel enrollment for those aged 45 and older into the scheme, if they happened to have recently altered their immigration status.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, long-time Citizens and residents remain grandfathered on the older, albeit discontinued ElderShield scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This effectively creates a disparity between older new Citizens and residents, and existing ones, if the latter had not opted into CareShield Life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Does the Ministry have any concerns over whether this disparate treatment might become an issue in the future?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, would it not be better to compel all to move over to the new scheme?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, these amendments, along with those to section 6(4)(b), exclude those who are severely disabled from the scheme, unless approved by the Minister.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand the economic rationale for such exclusions: we do not wish to create a case of adverse selection, where those enrolled in the scheme are all already disabled, thereby rendering the risk-sharing aspect moot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, it remains a moral responsibility for society to take care of those that are already disabled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that the Government does have in place a multi-pronged approach for supporting such individuals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This includes taxpayer-funded, means-tested subsidies and grants, other supplementary insurance schemes, access to self-funded healthcare savings and a last-ditch safety net.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, I would appreciate a comparison of how those without CareShield Life coverage would fare, relative to those who would, otherwise, be reliant on piecing together these disparate sources of financial support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, it is unclear how the Minister will exercise the discretion afforded to him.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Are there specific conditions which would lead an individual to be approved or excluded?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will start by noting the slight difference in the six categories defined by MOH, relative to other standards out there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, our basic ADLs include a separate mobility function which, I believe, is a significantly higher bar than simply transferring.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It also strikes me as a greater hurdle than either hygiene and grooming, or continence, which are used by the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health or the Katz Index, respectively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They mainly describe aspects of physiological self-care but exclude important ancillary aspects of psychological or social behavior that are nevertheless necessary for independent living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I accept that it is not possible to cover every possible aspect of effective functioning, I believe that it is, nevertheless, important to recognise that such instrumental ADLs can be materially impacted after a critical illness, which is precisely the sort of circumstances where one would hope insurance protection kicks in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, dignified living in modern Singapore virtually requires that individuals be able to perform certain instrumental ADL tasks, such as preparing or purchasing meals, handling money and using transportation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The lack of mention of these activities in the evaluation criteria for disability coverage under CareShield Life is even starker, when such metrics are already being accounted for by certain local medical support organisations, such as Dementia Singapore and the College of Family Physicians.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is also a notably bipartisan concern, having been raised in the previous term of Parliament by Members from both sides of the House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Admittedly, including all instrumental ADLs in coverage will likely mean a larger risk pool, which could, in turn, materially raise premium.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But even if we do not go the full extent of including all on the list, which typically includes up to eight distinct tasks, activities, such as communication, transportation and medical management, appear to be functions that are much more necessary for living in a modern city state, such as Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, using an index approach, it is possible to construct outcomes where those who qualify for CareShield Life as severely disabled might even score higher on an index of daily functioning than someone else who would have scored lower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we take the notion of disability assessment seriously, we should, perhaps, move away from the current binary outcome, like the inability to perform at least three ADLs, toward a more clinically corroborated approach that relies much more on index scoring.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The use of indexes is relatively widespread in jurisdictions, including Australia, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These have, directly or indirectly, been informed by my interactions with residents in Sengkang that have faced difficulties associated with the current operation of the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first concern is related to the optional enrollment process for those born 1979 and earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, some appear not to have fully understood what they are truly getting themselves into, in terms of their ongoing premium payments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I understand that underwriting principles require that participants be ultimately locked in, I wonder if the free-look period may be extended to a longer duration, such as three months.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, would it be possible for enrollees to opt out within, say, a year, perhaps with some penalty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, while optional exits would undeniably mess with actuarial calculations, opting out tends to be far less distortionary for the long-run financial viability of the fund, compared to unrestricted opt-ins.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, the Government has assured the public that they will ensure that no one will lose coverage due to an inability to pay their premiums.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is something that the Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon had reiterated earlier on several times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is important, not least because cost of living pressures, while abating over the past year, remain a major concern for many Singaporeans, and the last thing we would like to do is to saddle our workers with yet another cost increase, at a time when they are also simultaneously concerned about job security.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, would this support kick in, in the event that they lose their job, so that they do not also risk losing their insurance coverage at the same time?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I ask this because, to my knowledge, other insurance programmes run by the CPF Board, such as the Dependents' Protection Scheme (DPS) or the Home Protection Scheme (HPS), appear to be administered by companies such as Great Eastern and Income Insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have encountered instances where residents expressed dismay about how they were caught unaware that there were lapses in their coverage of either DPS or HPS, due to insufficient funds remaining in their CPF Ordinary Accounts (OA).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This was already discussed this morning by Minister Tan See Leng.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, while it is possible that some may be surreptitiously trying to reinstate their insurance plan ex post facto, to make a claim after an untoward event.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is, in fact, another plausible reason: because premiums had previously been automatically deducted from their CPF OAs, they did not meticulously track the need to routinely make payments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They were, thus, unaware when, due to inadequate OA balances, that their coverage had lapsed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, because they were expecting a contractual relationship with the Government and not a private entity, they then proceeded to overlook reminder mailings sent by these companies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will ensure that policyholders treat such correspondence seriously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, CPF must assure the public that, despite being managed by a non-Governmental entity, claims will continue to be evaluated not just with an eye toward prudence but also compassion and common sense.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will ensure that the hard-won trust of Singaporeans in the institutions of Government is not inadvertently squandered by private corporations that are chasing a bottom line.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, we must understand that the promises of CareShield Life to help the most vulnerable in our society to continue living a life of dignity after a devastating accident will only go so far as this is truly realised in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If support is too meager, too perfunctory or too grudgingly provided, then this promise will ultimately ring hollow.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This Bill continues the Government's careful and compassionate work to strengthen our national framework of long-term care, ensuring that no Singaporean faces the challenges of severe disability or extended care needs alone.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It reaffirms our social compact, that as we build a more inclusive "we first" society, we also build systems that allow Singaporeans to age with dignity, security and peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This of course reflects the way that Singaporeans increasingly communicate, ensuring that administrative processes keep pace with technological advancements.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These legislative enhancements coincide with significant policy shifts as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, this amendment reflects that the Government's care for the elderly and persons with disabilities, and demonstrates our society's sense of responsibility and foresight when facing the challenges of an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As society rapidly ages, more and more families will face the pressure of long-term care.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Whether due to age-related disability, or mobility difficulties caused by illness or accidents, long-term care is no longer "someone else's problem", but rather "a common issue for all of us".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This amendment makes the definition of "disability" clearer and more consistent, whilst also ensuring that document servicing channels are more convenient and effective.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Although these amendments appear to be technical, they concern whether families can receive timely assistance and protection in their caregiving journey.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I also hope that when the Government implements electronic servicing, it can consider the actual circumstances of elderly people and vulnerable groups, avoiding situations where they miss important information due to the digital divide.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can combine physical letters with social media to ensure no information is missed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Most importantly, we must continue to make "dignified ageing" our goal, establishing a reliable and compassionate long-term care system that allows every citizen to face the future with peace of mind. : While I support the Bill, I would like to raise a few clarifying questions and suggestions to strengthen its implementation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On the new "not disabled" definition: some individuals have progressive or cognitive disabilities that do not neatly fit into the six ADLs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will MOH issue updated clinical guidance and ensure that our assessors receive the adequate training to apply the criteria consistently?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Appeals processes should also be transparent and timely.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Clearer public guidelines with case examples and possibly tele-assessments for bedridden patients will reduce stress for families.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The shift to digital service is practical, but many affected groups are seniors with limited digital literacy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will MOH ensure that they are not disadvantaged by missed notices?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A "phygital" model should be the default for critical documents, such as demand notes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Community partners, such as the Silver Generation Office, the Infocomm Media Development Authority, media literacy ambassadors and the Community Development Councils (CDCs) can support vulnerable groups in managing their digital interactions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Regular public actuarial reports, similar to CPF's, can build trust.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: MOH could also consider more progressive subsidies for middle-income families who may not qualify for help but still shoulder heavy caregiving burdens.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: CareShield Life also operates in conjunction with many other schemes such as the Home Caregiving Grant and Medisave withdrawals for long-term care.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How will MOH ensure that families experience these as a coherent ecosystem, rather than fragmented programmes?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A one-stop care portal perhaps, that integrates financial, medical and social services could be a meaningful difference for families navigating sudden disability events.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On monitoring and review, what are the mechanisms that will be available to monitor the impact of these changes over the next few years?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Regular publication of disability assessment data, appeals statistics and processing times will also strengthen transparency.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ultimately, social and health initiatives often compete for limited fiscal space and must demonstrate measurable outcomes within short cycles.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, long-term care, by its very nature, requires patient sustained investment in our caregivers, in community infrastructure, and preventative programmes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We must continue to find ways to bridge support gaps through deeper partnership, flexible funding models and a mindset that sees care not as a cost but as a shared responsibility and a social investment in our collective future.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: CareShield Life is also ultimately very important as part of our care framework.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But by its very nature, it is abstract and its technical design makes it difficult for many to understand.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Compared to ordinary health insurance, disability-type insurance is less intuitive to many people.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is hard to internalise eligibility criteria, payout triggers, limitations on how premiums evolve.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And therefore, this requires much more public education.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And I do urge the Ministry to continually inform and educate our public on the importance of CareShield Life and how it operates.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed enhancements reinforce Singapore’s commitment to inclusive and future-ready care.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: CareShield Life offers lifetime monthly payouts for those who are severely disabled.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This goes some ways to help families manage the emotional and financial weight of caregiving.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Scheme is based on our ethos of shared responsibility – where individuals, families and the Government co-contribute to care financing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed amendments clarify the eligibility criteria of CareShield Life for the Optional Group – those born in 1979 or before, or aged 46 and above in 2025.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The intent is to ensure fair and consistent eligibility and claims for the cohort while balancing inclusivity with scheme sustainability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as we refine CareShield Life, we must also examine the lived realities of those navigating it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while I support the proposed amendments, there are a few points I would like to speak on: one, the underwriting criterion for the Optional Group and the implications for them; two, the affordability of premiums for retirees without subsidy support Given the importance of coverage for severe disability and to encourage more in the Optional Group to sign-up for CareShield Life, currently those with milder forms of disability can sign up for CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And as the Senior Minister of State has shared, this was a very deliberate decision to allow for some limited time for people to sign up.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the proposed amendment, eligibility now is tied to their disability status.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This means that they can only enrol in CareShield Life if they do not have any pre-existing disability as defined in clause 8 of the Bill and the new Fourth Schedule.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The definition states that a person is “not disabled” if he or she is able to do all of the ADLs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This intent is to prevent adverse selection risk, where those who are more likely to claim, opt in for CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do agree with the rationale for this stricter definition as it provides clarity of eligibility as it also prevents adverse selection risk.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will keep the scheme fair and more importantly, more sustainable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It does however mean that those in the Optional Cohort with mild disability, who would have qualified under the current time-limited requirements of mild disabilities will now not be able to be covered.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And as the Senior Minister of State has shared, this is concerning because one in two individuals in their lifetime will encounter severe disability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These individuals may need the coverage as they age.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: That being the case, we still have 900,000 not covered, and some of them may not have opted in due to perhaps not fully understanding the scheme and therefore not having the coverage.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I know that there has already been time given, but I do suggest and I do think that we must do more to help them navigate the full sweep and to understand the caregiving support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am not suggesting that we force this group to sign up, but what I think we have to do is ensure that people understand the full sweep of the Government schemes available so that they can make more informed decisions and more confident decisions for their long-term care financing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I know that the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) today, as well as the Silver Generation Office play a central role in providing resources and helpline to reach out and help families understand care options, eligibility and application processes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think more of us in the community need to understand these care options better and to help seniors with low digital literacy and also their caregivers understand the suite of long-term care financing support schemes available.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It matters because it helps bridge the last mile of families who lack coverage and who may not proactively seek help as they may be unaware or just too overwhelmed with their caregiving needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
