text: The affordability of CareShield Life premiums is tightly coupled with the Bill which lays the ground work for the enhancements proposed by the CareShield Life Council, which the Government has accepted fully.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And this includes the recommendation for higher payouts and correspondingly higher premiums to keep the scheme sustainable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There is concern about affordability of long-term care for those who do not qualify for subsidy support, particularly retirees.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These are often individuals who own modest assets but have limited cash flow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They fall just outside the means-tested thresholds, are caregivers for spouses or ageing parents while managing their own health.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The amount of increase may be small, but the retirees who are cash stretched that are not eligible for subsidy support for premiums, the increases may risk them opting out of the scheme even though they may be eligible and are vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given the higher property valuation in recent years, this impacts those living in modest private property with no income and who wish to age in place.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I know that the Senior Minister of State did give multiple reassurances that no one will be denied of CareShield Life coverage if they cannot afford the scheme, but this goes beyond just CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The principles of supporting our caregivers and their families goes beyond just the CareShield Life premium.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I do encourage that we continue to review and refine the criterion as we go.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We encourage families to be the main caregivers for their family members.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my engagement with our residents, it is heartening to see many families care of their elderly parents, siblings or relatives with disabilities and they live together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If they are living in a private property, AV is used for means testing and they are not eligible for the subsidy support for long-term care if they live in a private property, which generally, in my ward, falls beyond the current threshold.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can MOH consider refinement with the use of AV?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Refining AV as a criterion for means testing for long-term care support is vital for our policies to keep pace with the evolving demographics and caregiving realities as Singapore's population ages.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will still preserve our ethos of shared responsibility, where individuals, families and the Government co-contribute to care financing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It provides financial assurance at a time when care needs are high and income may be low, helping families manage the costs of home care, nursing services or caregiver support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Yet, we must ensure that Singaporeans understand that CareShield Life does not stand alone.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is complemented by a suite of targeted schemes like MediSave Care, which allows monthly withdrawals for care expenses; the Home Caregiving Grant, which offsets informal caregiving costs; and the ElderFund, which provides discretionary support for those with limited income and family help.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Together, these schemes form a layered safety net that ensures affordability, dignity and inclusion across diverse care settings and life stages.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I support the amendment as it ensures affordability and sustainability of CareShield Life while balancing inclusivity of the scheme.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These enhancements strengthen our long-term care system and give Singaporeans assurance that as our population ages, our system will remain robust, sustainable and responsive to evolving care needs such as the increased popularity of home caregiving services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As our national insurance scheme for severe disabilities above the age of 30, CareShield Life plays an important role in helping to defray the costs of long-term care, having evolved from the ElderShield scheme from earlier days.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will mean that persons with existing disabilities born before 1980 will not be able to join the scheme.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But when we look at the bigger picture, this will help with reducing the uncertainty when the actuaries are calculating the premiums and thereby reducing the extent of premium increases for everyone in the Optional Cohorts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am heartened to know that there will be other long-term care subsidies and grants available to them, such as the Home Caregiving Grant.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to ask if the Government has data on the percentage of this group who has made other plans to pay for the provision of long-term care, such as private insurance, and whether these plans are deemed sufficient.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: CareShield Life is designed to provide basic financial support and reduce out-of-pocket expenses should an insured develop severe disability and need long-term care.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For people that have to make a claim under CareShield Life, there could be other costs that cannot be fully covered by CareShield Life payouts, especially if they did not purchase a CareShield Life supplementary plan.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In effect, while CareShield Life helps to defray the costs of long-term care, Singaporeans will have to continue to ensure that they have enough savings or funding sources to afford the type of long-term care that they need and not assume that the insurance scheme will take care of everything.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the Government can consider raising public awareness about the types of costs that are associated with long-term care and the kinds of support that are available to them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   While CareShield Life helps to defray the costs of long-term care, Singaporeans will have to continue to ensure that they have enough savings or funding sources to afford the type of long-term care that they need and not assume that the insurance scheme will take care of everything.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the Government can consider raising public awareness about the types of costs that are associated with long term care, and the kinds of support that are available. : In conclusion, Mr Speaker, CareShield Life's long-term sustainability faces challenges from our ageing population, rising care costs and the limited coverage relative to actual expenses.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Continued Government oversight and actuarial reviews will be essential to maintaining a balance between the adequacy of benefits and the affordability of premiums over the coming decades.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What makes Singapore a truly first world country, having systems in place to ensure we can place those who mean the world to us first.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is what truly makes us a first world society.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Thus, I appreciate the Government's unwavering commitment to ensuring that CareShield Life remains a cornerstone of Singapore's social protection framework.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, as we move forward with these important refinements, particularly the modification of underwriting criteria, I believe it would be prudent for this House to understand the potential implications.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I fully appreciate that these changes are necessary to prevent adverse selection and maintain actuarial fairness, I would like to seek clarification from the Minister on specific areas of concern.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What might be the potential long-term impact of societal and healthcare costs of disability of persons excluded from the scheme?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How would this definition be applied to individuals with temporary disabilities or fluctuating or intermittent medical conditions?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Thirdly, for those who are excluded, but may apply for coverage, what are the conditions determined by the Minister, and what are the factors and considerations the CPF board will take into account in exercising its discretion under section 6(4B) of the act to grant an approval.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The streamlined assessment processes and expansion of accredited assessors will, undoubtedly, reduce burdens on families during their most difficult times.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It demonstrates that we can strengthen our schemes' sustainability, while deepening our support for those who need it most.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The balance between fiscal responsibility and social protection is commendable and necessary for the long-term viability of our social safety nets.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my maiden speech, I describe caregiving as a relentless wind buffeting a tree in a storm.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Its light must reach everyone, especially those navigating the toughest waters.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we refine the system, let us ensure that no one drifts unseen beyond its beam of protection.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With these questions, I look forward to the Minister's reply and further details on the measures to safeguard the inclusivity and effectiveness of CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Notwithstanding the questions I have raised, I commend the Minister and his team for their thoughtful approach to these complex challenges and support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Before I begin, I wish to declare that I am an orthopedic surgeon in practice and, from time to time, I do medical assessments for permanent disability.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I rise in support of the CareShield Life and Long-Term Care (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I want to first start commending the Ministry of Health, our public officers and the CareShield Life Council for continually refining this critical social protection framework that safeguards Singaporeans against the long-term financial impact of severe disability.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: CareShield Life is not merely an insurance scheme but one of the key pillars of our health and social security ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It reflects our collective commitment to care for one another, not only in good health, but also when illness or disability affects our independence and dignity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This Bill, by updating definitions, clarifying administrative provisions and streamlining service processes, demonstrates the Government's responsiveness to demographic shifts and societal change.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: While I broadly support the Bill, I would like to raise several suggestions for consideration, really aimed at strengthening the fairness, inclusion and sustainability within the CareShield Life framework.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The date an individual becomes a Singapore Citizen or Permanent Resident.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This clause rightly ensures that automatic coverage applies only if the person is not disabled at that point, safeguarding the integrity and sustainability of the insurance pool.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, this may unintentionally exclude long-serving residents who attain citizenship or permanent residence later in life, after decades of service, taxes and social contribution.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: By the time they become Singaporeans or Permanent Residents, some may already have developed chronic or mobility-related conditions.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For such individuals, the inability to access CareShield Life coverage can leave them feeling vulnerable and dependent on family or charity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I would, therefore, urge the Ministry to consider a transitional enrolment mechanism, perhaps through a time-limited transitional enrolment window with medical review or a subsidised premium buy-in or a limited base-coverage plan for those with pre-existing conditions.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This would combine fairness across cohorts and affirm our ethos that contribution to society should never go unrecognised.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As we know, dementia progressively affects memory, reasoning and daily functioning, often leaving the person dependent on full-time care.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Yet, under current arrangements, dementia patients do not automatically qualify for CareShield Life claims and must, first, undergo a severe disability assessment to determine the impact of dementia or cognitive impairment on their functional abilities.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This would affirm the dignity of those living with dementia and provide greater peace of mind to caregivers – many of whom are already ageing spouses or adult children managing multiple responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Recognising dementia under CareShield Life would bring policy coherence and, importantly, compassion into one framework.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: While we have made commendable progress in destigmatising mental illness and expanding community mental health services, the CareShield Life framework remains primarily oriented around physical disability, although our National Mental Health and Well-Being Strategy rightly emphasises holistic recovery.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Yet, for many individuals, mental illness can be equally disabling, preventing them from working, maintaining self-care or even engaging socially.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Conditions, such as severe depression, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, can become long-term and debilitating.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In fact, as an example, one of my Jurong Spring residents often comes to me complaining that her 19-year-old nephew, due to schizophrenia, basically lies in bed for 18 hours a day, similar to many patients with physical disability, and this takes a toll on her as a single caregiver.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I would suggest that the Ministry explore ways to include mid- to severe-level mental illnesses within the Act's coverage parameters, based on formal and structured psychiatric assessment.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These, of course, could be assessed by psychiatrists.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: By integrating mental health conditions into our longer-term care framework, we send an important signal that mental wellness is not peripheral to healthcare but central to human dignity and societal participation.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This would also encourage early intervention, continuous treatment and family support, key tenets of our national mental health strategy.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This same spirit of simplification can extend to the claims interface itself.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Currently, caregivers of severely disabled or dementia-afflicted family members must navigate multiple forms, medical reports and appeals, often while juggling employment and caregiving duties.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This process can be exhausting, especially when they are elderly caregivers who are not digitally fluent.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Such streamlining would not only reduce the administrative friction but also convey empathy through design, ensuring that our social insurance processes are as humane as the principles behind them.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Ultimately, a compassionate policy must also feel compassionate in process.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Members Mr Ng Chee Meng, Ms He Ting Ru and Ms Yeo Wan Ling reiterated this in their speeches earlier.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many Singaporean families are quietly performing full-time caregiving roles at home, often without formal training or respite.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They manage medications, behavioural changes and physical lifting, sometimes for years.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Recent heartbreaking cases remind us of the quiet struggles many caregivers face and the question that lingers is, who will look after the vulnerable when caregivers themselves can no longer do so?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Such coordination would reflect a care partnership model, recognising that the caregiver's well-being is a crucial part of the patient's recovery and quality of life.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As our society ages, empowering caregivers will become as important as funding the care itself.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: By doing so, we move closer to a society that values every life, not just for its productivity, but also for its humanity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: From insurance to assurance, that should be the next chapter of CareShield Life.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This first major review since 2020 strengthens a safety net that more families will rely on in the years ahead.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am also reassured that premiums remain fully payable by MediSave, because, at its heart, a national safety net must be accessible to all where no one should lose coverage simply because they cannot afford to pay at a point in time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By 2026, Singapore will be a super-aged society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As a labour Member of Parliament, I view this Bill through the lens of working families and caregivers on the ground.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My remarks focus on the "3As": Affordability, Adequacy, and Accessibility, with prevention, cost transparency, and the care workforce woven through each.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These measures are necessary, but they must also feel fair in real life, not just on paper.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For many self-employed and commission-based workers, their incomes swing month to month.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Means-testing should therefore reflect typical earnings over a reasonable period, rather than penalising a brief spike that nudges a family across a line.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Women often shoulder more caregiving and face career interruptions; we should continue monitoring women’s affordability and study targeted participation incentives for those who have prolonged caregiving spells, so premiums remain manageable without eroding retirement adequacy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Affordability also depends on families knowing what to plan for.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To give households and policymakers shared, reliable signposts, I propose an Annual Long-term Care (LTC) Cost and Workforce Report.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This should set out a simple, public “basic basket” of long-term care costs across home care, day care and nursing home settings, including transport and consumables, alongside wage and staffing trends in the care sector.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With clearer signals, we can calibrate subsidies early, rather than react late, and keep CareShield Life affordable and sustainable.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Sustained investment in promoting physical and mental well-being, chronic disease control, early rehab, and community health can delay or possibly avert disability and reduce time spent in severe disability.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Upstream health is not a slogan; it is the first pillar of affordability for our families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I urge MOH to continue keep scaling Healthier SG community programmes that help workers maintain good health and mental health, so they can stay employed longer and recover better if illness ever strikes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Keeping the claims threshold of three of six ADLs preserves affordability for the broadest base, while those who want earlier triggers can opt for supplement plans.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That balance between solidarity and choice is appropriate for a national scheme.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I note ground feedback that I have received from care workers and our unions that even with faster payout growth, the net dollar impact, after premium increases, may fall short for some families, and that some private supplements pay from one to two ADLs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While I support keeping CareShield Life affordable at three ADLs, I ask MOH to publish side-by-side publications, illustrations of premiums and payouts, base scheme versus supplements, so households can make informed choices.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Adequacy must keep pace with reality on the ground.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If care inflation or sector wage growth outstrips payout growth beyond 2030, we should be prepared to adjust the scheme parameters.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Annual LTC Cost and Workforce Report will give the Council and us in Parliament early warnings of cost and wage pressures, so refinements can be timely rather than overdue.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Adequacy rests on people, not just on numbers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When care workers are short-staffed or burnt out, our families end up paying more, paying more for private help or coping alone.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We should therefore scale workplace transformation through Company Training Committees, for example, workflow redesign, assistive technologies, tele-rehab and AI-enabled documentation, to lift productivity while protecting rest time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Crucially, productivity gains should translate into fair wages for care workers and tangible savings for families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A stable, respected workforce is how we keep services available at a standard and cost that families can live with.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Access should feel straightforward in moments that are anything but.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Where clinically appropriate, tele-assessments can spare less-mobile seniors and time-pressed caregivers additional trips.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Two refinements would make the process fairer without changing the ADL threshold: first, assessment guidance should explicitly recognise supervision needs arising from cognitive impairment or serious mental health conditions, so assessors apply criteria consistently and compassionately; second, repeat assessments should be waived or further subsidised when a condition’s trajectory is pretty clear, and recent specialist documentation should be accepted where appropriate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Alongside this, aligning eligibility rules, including property AV thresholds, would prevent families from qualifying for one scheme but missing out on another due to technicalities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill moves us in the right direction.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us pair it with the Annual LTC Cost and Workforce Report that I suggested, sustained workforce transformation that shares gains with both families and workers, and continued emphasis on prevention and mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This gives Singaporeans an important safety net, where long-term care will remain accessible and affordable, regardless of their pre-existing conditions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My speech today will touch on how we can better enhance these two key aspects of CareShield Life – accessibility and affordability.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Would the Minister be able to share statistics of Singaporean adults between 21 and 29 years of age, who have severe disabilities and are unable to perform at least three or more ADLs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Does this statistic differ substantially for the age group of adults between the ages of 30 and 39?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Ong has a 17-year-old son who has suffered an unfortunate brain injury and is therefore unable to engage in many ADLs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mr Ong must therefore expend significant resources, and he has done so to ensure that his son is well cared for.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Under the current scheme, Mr Ong’s son would only be able to enrol into CareShield Life when he turns 30.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I had written to MOH to highlight the plight of Mr Ong, and I understand from my resident that he was referred to caregiving support measures by the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) and ComCare, as his son does not meet the minimum age for CareShield Life enrolment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While I appreciate MOH’s assistance to the resident, the support provided by AIC and ComCare to Mr Ong are general schemes that would also apply to CareShield Life policyholders who are above the age of 30.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While such situations may be rare, I am certain that it is by no means unique.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Others like Mr Ong and his son would benefit from an expansion to the accessibility of the CareShield Life scheme, by lowering the minimum age of enrolment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Given the automatic enrolment nature of the CareShield Life scheme, I propose that we should have parity with other national insurance schemes that provide automatic insurance coverage.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For example, the CPF Board’s Dependants’ Protection Scheme (DPS), where automatic insurance coverage in the event of death, terminal illness, or total disabilities, is extended to Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents above the age of 21, with an option for manual application for those aged 16 and above.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We already have existing systems in place for family members to use their Medisave to pay for the CareShield Life premiums for other family members.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This can be extended to the younger cohort of policyholders that I am proposing for them to be covered by CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The various premium support measures by the Government for lower-income families can also be extended to policyholders below the age of 30, thereby ensuring minimum financial burden.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is vital to ensuring that CareShield Life payouts continue to defray a meaningful portion of long-term care costs and keep bills affordable for more Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is especially important as Singapore becomes a super-aged society, and our healthcare expenses continue to increase.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Singaporeans should not just rely on CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Indeed, many consumers already have private insurance policies to provide additional coverage in the event of a health incident that results in severe disability.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Despite this, insurance literacy in Singapore remains low.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is common to read in the media about consumers frequently being both under-insured where policyholders do not have adequate insurance coverage, and over-insured where policyholders have duplicate policies and excessive coverage amounts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Both situations of being under-insured and over-insured are not ideal, as it leads to policyholders paying more and increasing their financial burden over time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But it can be hard for consumers to cut through the noise when it comes to insurance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In closing, the amendments proposed under the Bill are timely, as it will help ensure that CareShield Life payouts continue to defray a sizeable proportion of healthcare costs for those who suffer severe disabilities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge MOH to expand the minimum age of enrolment for the scheme, to help young adults with disabilities and to improve insurance literacy among consumers.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: CareShield Life will play an increasingly vital role in our social safety net as we join the ranks of super aged societies.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a cornerstone of our national insurance framework, its financial support ensures that Singaporeans and Permanent Residents with severe disability and who require long-term care will have the funds to meet their care needs.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support the review and recommendations of the CareShield Life Council, which have been timely and necessary.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Its stance is balanced, weighing the need for sufficient payouts for essential care against affordable premiums.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: After this five-year financial support ends, how would the Government ensure that the premiums remain affordable?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the MOH consider premium discounts for policyholders who lead healthier lifestyles, such as abstention from smoking?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the Government's decision to improve and simplify the claims process and streamline applications across all national care schemes which the claimants are eligible for, as recommended by the Council.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of the Council's recommendations being considered by MOH is tele-assessments for claimants, in addition to those performed at their own residences, public hospitals and the assessors' places of practice, such as clinics.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When does the Ministry expect to conclude its feasibility study on this?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the assessors guard against fraud and potential misdiagnoses for tele-assessments?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Assessors play a pivotal role in the CareShield Life scheme, serving as the gatekeepers who determine eligibility for payouts based on an individual's ability to perform ADLs.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Their assessments directly impact the timeliness and fairness of financial support for those in severe disability, making their expertise and judgment essential to the integrity of the system.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we seek to improve the claims process and make it more claimant-friendly, it is timely to ask: what qualifications and training are required to become an assessor and how are we ensuring that there are enough assessors to meet growing demand?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would MOH provide a breakdown of the claimants by age groups of 10, for example, starting from age 30 to 40, 40 to 50 and so on; and by types of major causes, such as strokes, hereditary diseases and so on?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With these information, would it be possible to implement preventive measures to reduce the number of cases in each age and vulnerability group?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, would the Ministry share how many cases of appeal it had received in each of the years since CareShield Life started?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What were the percentages of successful and unsuccessful appeal cases?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What were the lessons learnt from these appeals and how has the Ministry improved on its assessment process?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must continue to review the scheme periodically to ensure that it serves our people expediently and compassionately in their time of need.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It helps residents keep pace with rising care costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, a scheme of this scale must be more than sustainable and fair in design.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It must also be compassionate and clear in execution.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With that in mind, I will raise four key areas for clarification.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An individual must now be able to perform all six ADLs without assistance, all the time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Under the new section 6(1)(b)(iii)(A), Singaporeans and Permanent Residents born before 1980 will be automatically enrolled only if they are not disabled when they first become citizens or Permanent Residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Those who are disabled at that time will not be automatically included.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, under section 6(4)(b), the CPF Board retains discretion to cover such individuals on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For those who became Singapore citizens or Permanent Residents before the commencement of this amendment, the earlier "not severely disabled" threshold will continue to apply.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This ensures continuity and fairness for those who entered the scheme under earlier rules.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Reinstating underwriting for older cohorts is understandable for financial sustainability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But it also risks leaving behind residents who are still in recovery.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A caregiver in Yio Chu Kang once told me about her husband's post-stroke journey: "Some days he can lift himself.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some days he cannot." Should a single assessment, taken mid-recovery, permanently close the door to protection?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the Ministry consider a more compassionate filter, such as, temporary waiting periods or premium loadings for manageable pre-existing conditions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This approach would allow recovery and inclusion to remain possible, while managing risk fairly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And for those still in rehabilitation, could there be a reassessment window, perhaps 12 to 24 months later, to give them a second chance once their condition stabilises?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Making a lifelong decision based on one judgment carries enormous weight.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What training and quality-assurance framework will ensure consistency, so that residents' futures are not determined by luck?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will MOH publish annual statistics on applications, acceptances, rejections and appeals for this older-cohort group?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will help the public monitor fairness and coverage over time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The "assess once, apply to many" approach reduces paperwork for families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But it also means that the result of a single assessment now carries more weight than ever before.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This phrase, now enshrined in statute rather than just clinical guidance, represents a significant tightening of the functional benchmark.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It may be precise, but it does not reflect the lived reality of many seniors whose abilities fluctuate from day to day.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some residents worry that outcomes can feel like a lottery – depending on who their assessor is, where the assessment is held, or even the time of day.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we assure them that the system sees people, not checkboxes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will MOH publish the clinical guidance and training protocols for accredited assessors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the results, such as inter-assessor reliability rates, be made public?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if a resident disagrees with an assessment, can they appeal directly through CPF Board channels?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond procedure, the assessment must capture lived reality.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A 30-minute clinical test cannot show how a senior manages narrow corridors, steep steps, or the absence of grab bars at home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can caregiver testimony and home-environment factors be formally considered as part of every assessment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A caregiver in Yio Chu Kang told me that bringing her frail mother across town for an assessment left both of them in tears.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To ease such stress, can MOH pilot video-based assessments for bedridden seniors, conducted with caregivers present?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To safeguard the integrity of ADL assessments, I suggest three measures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, a second assessment by another provider upon appeal, so no senior's fate rests on one single judgement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, formal integration of caregiver testimony into reports and third, public release of audit and appeal data to reinforce public trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I also note that under section 63 of the Act, the Minister may amend the Schedules – including this new Fourth Schedule – by order in the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This flexibility is important to ensure that our definitions of disability can evolve alongside medical knowledge and social realities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These clauses modernise how official notices, including demand notes, are served.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Importantly, the Bill now requires written consent, replacing the previous implied consent for email service.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Written consent may be given in either physical or digital form, but it must be explicit and verifiable, not assumed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Still, we must ensure seniors truly understand what they are consenting to.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will we protect seniors from replying to fraudulent emails that look official?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Under the new section 61A, a demand note can be served by post, by hand, by fax or by email.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To reduce confusion, can all demand notes, whether physical or digital, be written in plain language, in all four official languages and paired with an SMS alert?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A simple text saying, "You have an official notice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Please check your mailbox or MyInfo", can prevent panic and reduce the risk of scams.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Efficiency must never come at the cost of compassion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, to shift responsibility from seniors to the system, I would suggest for digital-only communication to be opt-in for residents aged 65 and above.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Those who are confident online can choose it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And those who are not, should continue receiving paper notices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be an automatic formula pegged to a dedicated long-term care inflation index?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Or will each adjustment still require a separate review?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To ensure payouts remain meaningful, could MOH set a public benchmark?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, anchoring benefits to a fixed proportion of median nursing home or home care costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry also consider a triennial actuarial review tied specifically to long-term care inflation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A predictable three-year cycle would make adjustments transparent and consistent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In estates like Yio Chu Kang, where senior density is high, residents worry not just about affordability but also availability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be enough home care slots, therapists and community-based services nearby?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But our task is not only to build a stronger system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is to build a more human one.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In my speech, we have spoken about fairness, making sure that older Singaporeans who are still recovering are not permanently excluded.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have spoken about compassion, ensuring disability assessments are consistent, holistic and grounded in the lived realities of our seniors and caregivers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have spoken about protection, guarding senior residents from confusion and scams as services move online.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And we have spoken about foresight, keeping CareShield Life sustainable and meaningful well beyond 2030.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are choices about the kind of society we want to grow old in, one defined by fairness, empathy and respect.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As policymakers, our responsibility does not end with legislation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It begins with listening, to every caregiver, every senior who worries about digital notices and every resident who wonders if the system will remember them when they grow old.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us make CareShield Life not just a financial safety net but a moral compact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One that says, in Singapore, we see our seniors not as dependents but as dignified individuals who built the foundation we now stand on.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And I thank them also for the thoughtful questions and useful suggestions they have given.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I have touched on some of these in my opening speech.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I will now elaborate more on those other areas that were raised by Members on three different areas: one, supporting Singaporeans with long-term care needs; two, keeping CareShield Life affordable and sustainable; and three, simplifying processes and improving access to financial support.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, on supporting Singaporeans with long-term care needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I have already explained this earlier but I think it is worth re-emphasising that CareShield Life cannot be seen in isolation.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It must be viewed alongside other layers of long-term care support, such as subsidies and grants, healthcare savings and social safety nets.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Ng Chee Meng and Ms Yeo Wan Ling will be heartened to know that the Government has been progressively enhancing these layers of support.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We enhanced the Caregivers Training Grant last year to better support individuals undergoing caregiver training.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Together, these enhancements to financing mechanisms complement each other to ensure that Singaporeans can access affordable long-term care when they need it most.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We recognise that Singaporeans have different long-term care needs and preferences.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As earlier mentioned, this is why we have made CareShield Life optional, for existing Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents born 1979 and earlier.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As for new Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents, they are required to join CareShield Life as part of the compact of becoming a new Singapore Citizen or Permanent Resident and this is made known to them at the point of application to be a citizen or a Permanent Resident.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Ng Chee Meng asked how the Government will ensure that CareShield Life payouts remain meaningful and adequate.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Council considered whether to make further enhancements to payouts, but was careful to balance benefit enhancements with premium affordability for policyholders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As part of the review, the Council consulted the public on a range of enhancement options through focus group discussions, including a higher payout growth rate.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, ultimately, there was recognition that premium affordability must remain a priority for our national scheme designed to provide basic coverage.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Council's recommendation therefore balanced the need for meaningful support while keeping CareShield Life accessible to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Nevertheless, those seeking more comprehensive coverage on top of CareShield Life and who are willing to pay higher premiums for this can consider privately-offered supplement products.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For the purpose of CareShield Life, the loss of three ADLs remains an appropriate threshold to indicate severe disability and higher care needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Alex Yam, Dr Wan Rizal and Dr Hamid Razak asked how CareShield Life supports those with cognitive disabilities and impairments, such as dementia patients, as they, too, have significant care needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOH's severe disability assessment framework does consider the impact of cognitive impairments on one's ability to independently perform an activity of daily living.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, an individual with severe dementia may physically be able to chew and swallow the food but may not remember how to do it without supervision.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This individual would be assessed to be unable to perform this ADL due to his cognitive impairment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And you can imagine, the same patient with dementia who may not be able to remember how to feed himself or herself could well also not remember how to dress himself or herself and may also have problems managing their toileting functions and, in which case, they will have crossed the threshold of three ADLs to qualify for payouts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Such individuals, therefore, can qualify for CareShield Life payouts when they are unable to perform three ADLs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked if the CareShield Life mandatory enrolment age can be lowered from age 30 to 21, with an optional enrolment application for those aged 16 and above.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CareShield Life policyholders pay premiums during their working years for protection against severe disability, which occurs mostly at older ages.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mandatory coverage begins at age 30 as most Singaporeans would have started work by then, have some income and savings in their MediSave accounts so they can use these MediSave savings to pay for their premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is a design feature of CareShield Life to make sure that it is something that is affordable, that those who have begun working for some time will begin to be able to service their premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will push up premiums for everyone else in that cohort.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There is a clear trade-off here and such a move needs to be considered very carefully.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But I would like to assure Members that young Singaporeans with disability requiring assistance to perform their ADLs, can access other Government schemes besides CareShield Life and these include, long-term care subsidies and grants, such as the Home Caregiving Grant, as well as safety nets, such as MediFund.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, we will make sure that care is affordable and is accessible to everyone.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Second, on keeping CareShield Life affordable and sustainable.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Members would appreciate that for any insurance scheme to be sustainable, enhancements in benefits must be accompanied by a corresponding adjustment in premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Several Members who spoke earlier made this point as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This includes transitional premium support to spread out and slowly phase in the increase over the next five years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Lower- and middle-income policyholders will see even lower premium increases, as they will enjoy further subsidies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Ng Chee Meng, Ms Joan Pereira and Dr Choo Pei Ling asked how we can keep premiums affordable even after this transitional support ends.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Beyond the transitional support, MOH will continue to provide means-tested premium subsidies for lower- and middle-income policyholders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will offset up to 30% of their premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Premiums will also continue to be fully payable by MediSave, with additional support provided to those with lower MediSave balances.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Recently, in July 2025, the Government provided MediSave top-ups of about $320 million to 600,000 Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Lastly, there is also the Additional Premium Support for policyholders, which Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked about.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will extend invitations to policyholders who are unable to afford their CareShield Life premiums even after subsidies and family support to apply for this additional premium support.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Dr Wan Rizal have asked about the means-testing framework.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In particular, concerns have been raised on whether the current approach towards considering property AV disadvantages some policyholders, such as in a scenario in which policyholders receive less subsidies after retirement when they no longer earn an income.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, in general, policyholders from lower-income households receive more premium subsidies than those from higher income households.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For most policyholders, there will be no more premium payments after retirement, as CareShield Life premium payments currently end at age 67.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is pegged to the re-employment age in 2020 when the scheme was launched.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, the issue of a retiree living in a private property with high AV is not really relevant here.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Most of them, by that age, would have stopped paying premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Only a small group of individuals in the Optional Cohort, who had chosen to opt-in at older ages, would have to pay premiums beyond age 67.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We, likewise, support eligible individuals through premium subsidies and, in addition, those who joined before 31 December 2024 would have also been receiving additional participation incentives of up to $4,000 in total, to offset their premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Should anyone still face difficulty paying premiums after subsidies and other support, the Government will provide Additional Premium Support to fully cover their premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I say again, to fully cover the premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is why I keep saying to Members that no one will lose CareShield Life coverage due to an inability to pay their premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Ms He Ting Ru and Dr Wan Rizal raised concerns about premium affordability for women.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This was also discussed extensively in this House in 2019 when CareShield Life was first introduced.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In general, within any insurance risk-pool, premiums are actuarially priced such that the premiums collected can pay out for expected claims.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is the case for both men and women.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Here, gender is a relevant factor for CareShield Life as the key parameters that affect long-term care insurance claims such as lifespans, duration and likelihood of disability do vary between men and women.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Women tend to live longer than men and are more likely to develop severe disability, and therefore are more likely to stay in disability for a longer period.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This has remained the case in the past few years too.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It will mean that in the event of a severe disability, a woman will typically receive CareShield Life payouts for a longer duration.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Support is available for women in lower-income households through existing support schemes, including premium subsidies and Additional Premium Support.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Beyond these measures to ensure premium affordability for those who need more support, there is also a need to ensure that the long-term trajectory for CareShield Life premiums remains sustainable and affordable for all policyholders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I listened to Ms He Ting Ru's speech, I got the sense that she has not quite grasped the features of CareShield Life.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There are two distinct features in CareShield Life that are quite different from all other insurance schemes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The first is that this is a cohort-based risk pooling.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In other words, the risk-pooling happens in your age cohort.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is not whole-population risk pooling, it is risk pooling among those who are born in the same birth year.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It means that the burden of any premium that needs to go up is borne by a lower number of people, just in that age cohort alone.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The second feature is that this is a pre-funded scheme with limited premium contribution duration but has a lifelong payout as long as a person remains in disability.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I said earlier, women do live longer and reach older ages where severe disability becomes more likely.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We can all understand that as one ages, at older ages, women are 10% more likely than men to enter severe disability at a given age.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is not about discriminating women, this is just biology.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As you get older, as you live longer, you are just at a higher risk for many other health problems.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Women are at a higher risk of getting osteoporosis compared to men.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They are therefore more likely to get severe hip fractures when they sustain a fall and they may remain disabled for a far longer period of time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If I can just contrast the design of CareShield Life with MediShield Life, which will hopefully illustrate why there is that gender differentiation in the premium.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MediShield Life policyholders pay premiums for life as opposed to CareShield Life, where you stop paying when you reach 67.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This means that for MediShield Life, there is no need to insure against the different life expectancies across genders, because the premiums are payable for every year of coverage.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If you live longer, you just pay more premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CareShield Life, as I have said, one of the features is that it is pre-funded – for a limited duration, while one is working.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Over a lifetime, while women may make more claims due to a longer life expectancy, they will also have to pay more for their premiums because there is the only fair principle.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If you are going to claim more and claim for longer, one pays more during the contribution years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is not about discriminating women or being unfair to women.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is also being fair to the men.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Remember, this is about risk-pooling within one cohort, with a limited number of people sharing the risk and therefore, maintaining the payouts for that cohort that needs to claim.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A key change that we are introducing through this Bill is intended to safeguard the sustainability and affordability of CareShield Life.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: By restoring the underwriting criteria for the scheme, we will lower premiums for older Optional Cohort policyholders who today pay higher annual premiums than the mandatory cohort policyholders who joined the scheme at a younger age.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I hear Ms Elysa Chen, Ms Jessica Tan and Dr Hamid Razak's concerns over whether reinstating underwriting criteria would make the scheme less inclusive.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This means that a young person in the mandatory cohort with preexisting disability will still be auto-enrolled when he turns 30 years old.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: He will pay the premiums for his age once on enrolment and if he is determined upon disability assessment to meet the three ADLs threshold for severe disability, he will be eligible for claims for life thereafter and stop paying further premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is how we make sure that the scheme is inclusive and takes care of those with needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For the Optional Cohort, those born in 1979 and earlier, we had provided a time-limited concession for those with mild or moderate disabilities to join the scheme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This concession, as I have said earlier, was originally intended to be for two years, up to 2023.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: After two years, we extended this concession to enable more to join in.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The extension enabled us to redouble our outreach efforts in the post-COVID-19 period.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We also extended the duration of participation incentives and conducted extensive outreach to seniors to encourage them to join.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In fact, the concession period lasted for about four years in total.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If we were to include those who chose to remain on ElderShield, about seven in 10 older Singaporeans are enrolled in our national long-term care insurance schemes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will moderate the premium impact for all Optional Cohort policyholders, keeping the scheme fair and sustainable.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To keep the scheme fair, this approach will be taken for new Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents of the same age groups as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar, Ms He Ting Ru, Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Elysa Chen asked whether there have been sufficient provisions made for those in the Optional Cohorts who may have chosen not to enroll in CareShield Life.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As mentioned in my opening remarks, there are different layers of financial support for those who require long-term care.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Individuals may have chosen to prepare for and pay for their long-term care in other ways, such as through personal savings or private insurance.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For those who are not enrolled in CareShield Life, there continues to be other layers of support, such as subsidies and grants, which have been significantly enhanced recently.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I hope this addresses Ms He Ting Ru's concerns.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOH will continually review our financing schemes to ensure that long-term care costs remain affordable.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Another change we are making through this Bill is to strengthen our provisions for premium recovery.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I want to assure Mr Alex Yam and Mr Yip Hon Weng that physical notifications will continue to be sent to all policyholders where necessary, including those who are less tech savvy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: More broadly, the changes are necessary to equip our administering agencies with tools to recover premiums that are due.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Without such tools, premiums owed by wilful defaulters will become bad debt, which will be borne as higher premiums by other policyholders in that cohort.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is unfair to those who have been responsibly paying their premiums.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Members have rightly observed that an ageing population and rising costs of care could present challenges to premium affordability over the long run.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We agree with Ms Mariam Jaafar that sustained investment in prevention and well-being is crucial.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government is paying close attention to these trends and has embarked on national strategies to address this.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This includes Healthier SG and Age Well SG, which aim to empower Singaporeans to live healthy and active lives.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: By staying in good health, we not only minimise the cost of care, but importantly, enable every Singaporean to live their lives to the fullest.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That in itself should be the biggest benefit to Singaporeans, although there are also other subsidies and incentives in place to promote preventive health.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Dr Choo Pei Ling suggested offering CareShield Life premium discounts for those who lead healthier lifestyles.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: At the heart of Dr Choo's question and suggestion is the principle that prevention is better than cure.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I had earlier shared the strategies the Government has rolled out to support healthy and active living.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOH had rolled out a premium discount pilot for MediShield Life just last month.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Unlike MediShield Life, CareShield Life is still a nascent scheme with just a few years of claims experience.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is especially since onset of severe disability typically takes place only at older ages and most CareShield Life policyholders are still young today.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, there is only limited data, including on how healthy behaviours translate to lower claims for severe disability.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: When more claims data is available, we can consider if similar premium discounts can be considered in future.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The CareShield Council will also review CareShield Life regularly over time to ensure that both the benefits and premiums, including the actuarial assumptions, remain relevant and sustainable over time as our demographic profile evolves.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Council regularly monitors the financial status of the CareShield Life and ElderShield Insurance Fund to ensure that premiums, which are set on a non-profit basis, remain adequate to sustain the scheme's obligations to all policyholders over time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In response to Ms He Ting Ru's question, I want to assure her that the information on the Fund, including the amount of claims and investment claims, is already publicly available in CPF Board's annual financial statements.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Third, on simplifying processes and improving access to financial support.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Before I elaborate further, let me just first clarify with Assoc Prof Jamus Lim that CareShield Life is administered by the CPF Board and not outsourced.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We fully acknowledge the challenges faced by caregivers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We are committed to improving the user journey for care recipients and caregivers and ensuring a citizen-centric experience that allows residents to get support in a timely manner, as Ms Mariam Jaafar has shared.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: More GPs in the community, therapists and nurses are being trained, and every public hospital now has in-house assessors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have also expanded the number of assessors who perform house calls to improve access and convenience for policyholders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOH and AIC will press on with efforts to expand our assessor pool.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I would also like to assure Mr Yip Hon Weng as well as other Members that we will continue to ensure that assessors are rigorously trained to conduct fair and high quality assessments.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These serve as a one-stop resource to help connect care recipients and their caregivers to the support they need.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our Silver Generation Ambassadors also reach out to seniors to explain schemes in a clear and more personal manner.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As Mr Melvin Yong and a number of Members have noted, better awareness and insurance literacy can help families make more informed financial decisions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Community touchpoints also continue to remain an important source of help for seniors and caregivers to understand the suite of long-term care financial support schemes available.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will continue to work with AIC and community partners to reach out to families to increase awareness of the support available.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We agree with Ms Mariam Jaafar that we can make our scheme application process more claimant friendly.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: One way we have done so is by giving residents the opportunity to be automatically assessed across various disability schemes after having undergone a disability assessment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This reduces the administrative burden and ensures timely support for families.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will continue to identify areas for improvement and ensure the claims process remains efficient and responsive to policyholders' needs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While we cannot stop time, we can shape how we age.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Government is taking steps to empower Singaporeans to lead active, healthy and purposeful lives in their silver years through national initiatives such as Age Well SG.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Some of us may come to require more support for our ADLs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our commitment to Singaporeans is that we will continue to develop our care ecosystem through more community care services and Age Well Neighbourhoods, to enable more to age-in-place confidently.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: He says that the AV is not relevant for retirees.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I would say it is relevant with regard to CareShield Life premium because the assumption is that people only retire at 67.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: But that is the reemployment age and many of my residents had to have to retire before that and they are in their early 60s; because either of poor health, sometimes because of caregiving needs because some of their family members require it so they do have to retire slightly earlier.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And some, their jobs are disrupted and for someone older, especially a matured professional, it is usually harder to get a job at that age.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And so, therefore, it is relevant, and they have no income and if they happen to live in a property that is just slightly above the threshold, they do not qualify.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: And it is not just for CareShield Life premium, but like I said, it is the same means-testing for across all the other long-term candidates so it sort of exacerbates the point.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: The Senior Minister of State, I hear him and I agree with him and I have his assurance on CareShield Life premium.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: I just hope that we look at it in a more holistic landscape.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: As the Senior Minister of State have said, long-term care is a larger framework and because the current support framework is based on that same criteria and therefore that is why I am harping on this point because it is a larger impact and I do see families, they are seniors themselves and they care for other seniors or families with disability and that little bit more support will make a big difference.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I have a couple of clarifications for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: The first being while we acknowledge that women are at risk of longer-term disability and living more years in ill health and this I acknowledged in my speech.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I think the point I was making is and this is why I raised the New South Wales study, which found that even though the level of disability in their case was about 50/50 between women and men, they found that women actually only made up for 37% of the claims and one of the reasons or the concerns raised there was that women were actually not, for whatever reason, not claiming as much.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: So, I was just wondering whether we are facing similar challenges here in Singapore and whether the Senior Minister of State can share some data about the differentiation between the claims because biology, lifespan, health span all that is one thing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: But, of course, what matters in the case of an insurance scheme is the actual claims and the actual data and who is actually claiming and for how long.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I think it would be helpful for the House to understand this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: And the second point would be about, again, more on the gender-differentiated premiums.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: I just wanted to note that yes, we understand, at least I understand that the cohorts is by age cohort and I think the point that I was making was how can we work towards making each cohort gender neutral?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But the way we do it, on your second clarification, was the fact that we use principles from actuarial science to actually price the premium based on the gender differences in their biological behaviour over time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And the Council is prepared to relook at actual data over time and decide if further adjustments are needed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Whether it will move towards completely equal parity between men and women, I do not know.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Maybe men will participate more in Healthier SG and become healthier, and they can live just as long.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We might reach parity but only time will tell how the data will pan out.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I wanted to follow up on the reinstatement of the underwriting criteria for the Optional Cohort.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: As we know this cohort is senior, you know, most of them are now in their 50s and 60s and I take the Senior Minister of State's point that the enrolment has dropped to a trickle, but I am concerned that the people who perhaps have not enrolled by now may fall more in the lower-income brackets who did felt that they did not have, you know, enough savings for the premiums or did not have the financial literacy for it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: And also, mild and undiagnosed conditions may be more common in those cohorts that are in the lower-income segments than others.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: So, it is a little bit of a concern to me that those are most likely to get screened out, and this applies to the Optional Cohort as well as the new Citizens.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: First, what assurances does the Senior Minister of State have that the underwriting process will be fair, transparent and medical robust?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: In particular, the borderline cases for the mild conditions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Second, will there be clear appeals or a second opinion pathway so that one assessment does not mean that somebody is excluded for life.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: And third, this one I raised and I did not hear a response to it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Do we really have to take this all-or-nothing approach?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Is there some way that you can consider some tiered or partial entry options for those who may have some mild disabilities and may be excluded under the underwriting criteria?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But let me just give some context to this because the Optional Cohort is the older cohort that is actually a much smaller cohort, because the number of people in that age range would be lesser than those in the younger cohort.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Member can imagine that as they age, less and less of their peers will be around.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Member understands the math behind it, yes?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I think in trying to help this Optional Cohort to be part of the CareShield Life we also have to consider what it means to the rest of them who are already in the same cohort who are CareShield Life policyholders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Because they are bearing a lot more premiums today in anticipation of someone who may choose to join much later on with disability.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I hope this is something that the Member can appreciate that, it is really striking the balance between wanting to help the remaining small number of people or to be fair to the rest of them who has already made the effort to come in and do the risk-pooling.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the second case of whether there is an appeal mechanism.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But, in general, severe disability, especially permanent disability does not really change over time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is why they are called permanent disability.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And if the assessment is that this is a permanent disability, generally, the assessor would have to be quite certain that it is a particular condition that will see no chance of improvement over time and it is something that we have to strengthen in terms of the training we provide to the assessor so they can make a clear, unbiased assessment of the level of disability to qualify for the three ADLs threshold that we talked about here and I hope that is something that will help to allay the Member's concerns about this particular aspect.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, and that is part of the reason why we are now tightening the underwriting and this is to respect the principles of making sure that it actually is sound and the underwriting is fair.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling
text: As mentioned in my earlier speech, one of the Council's recommendations being considered is tele-assessments for claimants.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling
text: Separately, I would also like to seek clarification on whether the Ministry would be able to share any cases of appeal it had received in the years since CareShield Life started?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling
text: And what were the percentages of successful and unsuccessful appeal cases?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the second one on cases of appeal, I do not have data on hand right now, so if she wants to know more, perhaps, she will have to file a Parliamentary Question at some other Sitting.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the tele-assessment, this is still very much a pilot at the moment, as Dr Choo would probably understand, assessing disability on the remote setting carries technical challenges.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The assessor on the other end of the line will have to first make sure that it is safe for the person with disability to be assessed without the assessor's assistance.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There could be a risk of falling, for example.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And also, you make sure that it is not something that can be gamed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, there are some real challenges and so this pilot will help us to understand what are the challenges we need to overcome, what are the safeguards we need to put in to make sure it is fair, to make sure it is something that is robust, before we can think of rolling this out in a broader way.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I hope the Member will give us a bit more time to take a look at what are the outcomes that the pilot shows before we can think about how to broaden it to wider application.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first builds on the question by Ms He Ting Ru about gender-neutral data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I appreciate Senior Minister of State Koh's explanation that CareShield is a brief programme, but we have a predecessor programme, ElderShield.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Although it is different, I wonder whether that longer history would afford us the ability to differentiate between the gender data that Ms He requested and if we do not have that on hand, perhaps if we should be filing a Parliamentary Question on this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My second question also riffs off a clarification by Ms Mariam Jaafar about the all-or-nothing approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I understand his clarification that we do not want to have a system where it is gamed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But one point that I raised in my speech was about an index approach, either Katz Index or modified Barthel Index would assign scores that differ according to whether it is moderate disability or severe disability, and then mapped those through an ultimate score.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That kind of scoring approach is purely objective and may rule out the possibility of this kind of gaming of the system.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, we can take a look and if there are data to share, we would do so maybe at a future Sitting.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I mentioned in my speech, the Council's decision is to take a balanced one where, as a basic level of protection for all Singaporeans, they want to make this affordable and more broad-based rather than opening up to a lot more claims and making it far more difficult for especially those in the lower income to be accessible.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And for those with milder disability, generally you can imagine that their care needs would be much lesser, in which case our approach of strengthening subsidies at the care delivery setting would make many of these care more affordable already and available to those in milder disabilities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it is not just trying to solve the problem with one tool but looking at the multiple layers of support we have, by first of all, making the overall care cheaper through subsidies, through grants so that the need to even tap on CareShield Life for milder, maybe to moderate, disability will be much lesser as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But allow me to clarify that actually using an index approach, you do not necessarily need to expand the coverage to individuals purely facing mild disabilities.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is also something that many of our clinicians and doctors are familiar with.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
